title: Execution invocation and outcome must be independently recorded, never inferred from scheduler-claimed state
requirement: Where a Clank fires collection or other scheduled work from any trigger mechanism (its own in-process scheduler, an OS-level scheduler, an external platform), the Clank MUST record, in its own stored data, two facts independently: (1) that an invocation occurred, and (2) what outcome that invocation produced. Neither fact may be inferred from scheduler-reported state alone (e.g. 'task enabled', 'next run scheduled', 'last exit code 0', 'timer active'). A cycle that correctly performs no work because nothing was due MUST be recorded as an explicit no-work outcome, not left as an absence indistinguishable from a materialization failure. A process starting MUST NOT, by itself, be treated as evidence that collection completed or succeeded.
trigger: Applies to any Clank that fires collection or comparable scheduled work from some trigger mechanism. Scheduler technology and its location (in-process, OS-level, external platform) are out of scope for this standard — the invariant binds the Clank's own recorded evidence of what happened after a trigger fired, not who or what did the firing. A Clank with no scheduled/triggered execution at all has nothing for this standard to bind.
rationale: Evidenced by the single most severe operational incident found in the fleet survey: a 2026-08-22 root-privileged redeploy silently broke cron execution across three Clanks simultaneously for approximately 36 hours, because scheduler invocations existed while zero application runs materialized and no failure record was written. Independently: a stale pre-migration cron launcher fired invisibly alongside a new scheduler architecture for days; a due-gating aggregation bug caused roughly four times the intended request rate for over a week while individual per-source due-checks were each correct; a single-worker scheduler process silently dropped 165 due executions under a misfire grace window. Five Clanks independently built distinct mechanisms addressing some part of this gap, and semiconductor-intelligence's invocation-vs-successful-commit split is already cited fleet-wide as a reference pattern. A rule here must not itself manufacture false positives: a real incident (a monitoring tool inferring a materialization gap from three genuinely empty, correctly-due-gated cycles) is directly guarded against by requiring a no-work cycle to be a recorded outcome, never an inferred absence.
forbidden: Presenting scheduler-reported state ('timer active', 'task enabled', 'next run scheduled') as proof that a collection cycle actually ran
Treating a process start, or an exit code alone, as evidence of a successful collection outcome
Leaving a legitimately empty, correctly-due-gated cycle unrecorded such that its absence is indistinguishable from a failure to materialize
Silently allowing a second, forgotten, or duplicate trigger source to fire against the same work without that duplication being detectable from recorded invocation evidence
acceptance: For any given trigger firing, a downstream reader can determine, from the Clank's own stored data, that an invocation occurred, independent of asking the scheduler
For any recorded invocation, a downstream reader can determine what outcome it produced (work performed, an error, or an explicit no-work determination), independent of the invocation record alone
An intended/scheduled execution is distinguishable from an actually-materialized invocation: 'the schedule says this should run' and 'this ran' are never conflated
A no-work outcome (nothing was due, nothing to collect) is represented as an explicit, positive outcome record, not as the mere absence of a work record
Two independent trigger sources firing against the same work are each independently visible in recorded invocation evidence, making duplicate/zombie automation detectable

evidence.summary: A 2026-08-22 root-privileged redeploy silently broke cron across three Clanks simultaneously for ~36 hours: scheduler invocations existed, zero application runs materialized, no failure record was written.
A stale pre-migration cron launcher fired invisibly in parallel with a new systemd-timer architecture for days, undetected because nothing compared the two invocation sources.

A whole-fleet AND-gated due-check meant one permanently-failing source kept the gate permanently due, running full cycles at ~4x the documented cadence for over a week despite each per-source due-check being individually correct.

A single-worker resident scheduler process silently dropped 165 due executions under its own misfire grace window; fixed by computing due-ness from stored run history rather than trusting in-memory scheduler state.

Persists scheduler invocation and successful job commit as two distinct, never-conflated fields; cited fleet-wide (clank-architecture Fleet Law 3, ADR-0002) as the reference semantic for this distinction.

A monitoring tool inferred a false-positive materialization gap from three legitimately empty, correctly-due-gated OEM Radar cycles that wrote no work row; fixed by introducing positive no-work-due evidence, never inferred from absence.
